text.p: The U.S. Justice Department said Thursday it has had "talks" with Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co., which has been accused of discriminating against minorities in selling homeowner policies in urban neighbourhoods.
"We are engaged in talks (with Nationwide) regarding allegations of discrimination," spokeswoman Lee Douglass said in a telephone interview. "The talks have been constructive."
Asked if a full-scale investigation is under way, she said the department does not confirm or deny any investigations.
Columbus, Ohio-based Nationwide, the sixth largest U.S. property/casualty insurer, said it was reviewing its urban marketing strategy. The company plans a news conference Friday.

"We are evaluating whether our underwriting guidelines constitute a barrier to our gaining market share in urban markets," Nationwide spokesman John Millen said in a telephone interview late Thursday.

A non-profit organisation, the National Fair Housing Alliance, said Nationwide makes it difficult or costly for homeowners in predominantly African-American, Hispanic or integrated urban neighbourhoods to insure their homes.
The group had homeowners in such neighbourhoods ask insurers for information, then had owners of comparable homes in mostly white, suburban neighbourhoods do the same.
"Our investigations have shown that Nationwide has engaged in discrimination in several ways," executive director Shanna Smith said in a telephone interview.

For example, an urban home might cost two to three times as much to insure as its suburban counterpart. In some areas, Nationwide would not insure homes valued at less than $60,000 or limit coverage on homes built before 1950, she said.
"That had a greater impact on integrated and minority neighbourhoods" since many urban homes are older and valued at less than similar suburban homes, she said.
Nationwide's Millen said its age and valuation guidelines were based on traditional industry standards.

Nationwide Insurance Enterprise's property and casualty companies, including Nationwide Mutual, are separate business units from a life insurance unit, Nationwide Financial Services, Inc., which plans a public offering of stock.
